nameStory: The "slender" in this woodsorrel's name refers to its delicate, thin stems and overall graceful appearance compared to its more robust cousins. "Woodsorrel" comes from the sour taste of its leaves - "sorrel" means sour in Old French, and these plants have been nibbled by forest wanderers for centuries. The scientific name honors Johann Jacob Dillenius, an 18th-century German botanist who was among the first to study and classify many small flowering plants.
description: Slender yellow woodsorrel is a small, low-growing plant that looks remarkably like a tiny clover at first glance. It produces delicate three-part leaves and cheerful yellow flowers about the size of a pencil eraser. This dainty plant rarely grows taller than your ankle, spreading along the ground with thin, wiry stems. You'll often find it popping up in gardens, sidewalk cracks, and woodland edges throughout New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three heart-shaped leaflets arranged like a shamrock, each about the size of your thumbnail. The leaflets feel soft and tender, and have tiny pointed hairs that give them a slightly fuzzy texture when you run your finger across the surface.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly five petals, each bloom smaller than a dime. The petals have a silky, delicate texture and the flowers often appear to glow in dappled sunlight.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive brown seed pods that are finger-shaped and about an inch long, standing upright from the stems. When ripe, they split open explosively when touched, shooting tiny seeds several feet away.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading plant with slender stems that feel slightly succulent and break easily. The whole plant has a delicate, almost translucent quality and rarely exceeds 6 inches in height.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves fold downward at night and in bright sunlight, like tiny umbrellas closing. They have a pleasant, lemony-sour taste when chewed and feel tender between your teeth.

habitat: Slender yellow woodsorrel thrives in disturbed soils and partially shaded areas throughout New England's lowlands and foothills. You'll commonly spot it in garden beds, along woodland paths, in sidewalk cracks, and at the edges of lawns where grass meets flower beds. It particularly loves areas with rich, moist soil that gets morning sun but afternoon shade.

seasonality.spring: Fresh green leaves emerge early, often while other plants are still dormant. The first yellow flowers begin appearing in late spring, creating cheerful dots of color in gardens and disturbed areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers appearing continuously. Seed pods develop and mature, ready to explode at the slightest touch by mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue flowering until the first hard frost. Seeds disperse throughout autumn, and the tender leaves turn slightly reddish before dying back completely.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible, but seeds lie dormant in the soil, ready to germinate when warm weather returns.

funFact: This plant is a natural catapult engineer - its seed pods can launch seeds up to 10 feet away when they explode, and the explosion happens so fast it's barely visible to the human eye, creating a tiny "pop" sound you can actually hear in a quiet garden!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with regular clover, but woodsorrel's heart-shaped leaflets (versus clover's oval ones) and yellow flowers (not white or pink) are dead giveaways. Memory trick: "Hearts are sour, ovals are sweet" - woodsorrel has heart-shaped leaflets and sour-tasting leaves, while clover has oval leaflets and isn't sour.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being labeled a "weed" by many gardeners, this plant is completely edible and has been used as a wild green and natural source of vitamin C for centuries. The sour taste comes from oxalic acid, the same compound that gives rhubarb its tartness, though it should only be eaten in small quantities.
compareHints: Slender yellow woodsorrel is smaller and more delicate than upright yellow woodsorrel, with thinner stems that tend to sprawl rather than stand erect. Unlike mountain woodsorrel which has white flowers with pink stripes, this species produces pure yellow blooms. It's also much smaller than great yellow woodsorrel and lacks the creeping, mat-forming habit of creeping woodsorrel.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mountain woodsorrel differs from its yellow-flowered relatives in the genus by having white petals with pink veins instead of bright yellow ones.
Among New England's woodsorrels, upright yellow woodsorrel stands tall while creeping woodsorrel sprawls flat along the ground.
Creeping woodsorrel differs from its upright cousin (Oxalis stricta) mainly in its prostrate, mat-forming growth habit versus the upright's tall, erect stems.
Violet wood-sorrel is easily distinguished from its New England relatives by its purple flowers - all other common wood-sorrels in the region have yellow flowers.
Unlike other woodsorrels in New England which have green leaves and yellow flowers, false shamrock stands out with its deep maroon foliage and white or pink blooms.
Among New England's woodsorrels, this is the only one with large pink flowers - all the others have either small yellow blooms or purple ones.
Great yellow woodsorrel differs from its more common relatives like upright yellow woodsorrel and slender yellow woodsorrel by its significantly larger leaflets and more spreading growth habit.
Pink-sorrel stands out from New England's other woodsorrels primarily by its pink flowers - most relatives have yellow blooms, while violet woodsorrel has purple flowers.
